documentation.rationale: Identity and terms are excellent: VIN corroborated three ways, Porsche Certificate of Authenticity confirming Lapis Blue/Stone Gray and factory options, Carfax snapshot, BaT sale history including the $28,000 October 2022 result, named dealer, $0 additional dealer charges, and a stated auction close. Maintenance and condition evidence is genuinely present but thin at the top end: three dated invoices 2024-2026, a VIN-matched DME over-rev scan, a 2011 accident repair order, paint-meter photos in the gallery, and an in-house checklist. What is missing is the expensive half — no borescope, no cooling/AOS/water-pump history, nothing documenting the first 17 years and 62,000 miles beyond the claim that records from new exist, and no follow-up invoice proving the May 2026 misfire was cured. Two internal conflicts (brake and tire measurements) also undercut the dealer checklist's reliability.

condition.rationale: Presentation is strong: paint in the photos looks deep and consistent across panels, panel gaps at the hood and decklid look even, the 18in wheels are unkerbed with matching Michelin PS4S on all four corners, the Stone Gray seats show no bolster collapse or cracking, and the underbody photo shows clean, uncorroded trays, arms and exhaust with no staining around the engine undertray. Against that: a documented cylinder 1/3 misfire four months before the sale with no documented verification of the fix, a car that has covered roughly 1,000 miles in four years (seals, AOS diaphragm, tires and fluids age regardless), brake pads flagged at 4mm to sensor in February 2026 and unexplainedly reported at 7/6mm in August, and no independent assessment of the single most expensive failure mode on this engine. Unknown cylinder-wall condition pulls this down hard on an M97 3.4.

price_value.rationale: The $5,105 shown is an opening-week bid with four bids and six days left, not a market signal. Comparable 987.1 S manuals are settling at $23,250 (2006, 103,700 mi, CA), $27,750 (2007, 97,700 mi), $29,500 (2007, 40,000 mi, San Jose) and up, with a 28,000-mile car failing to meet reserve at $27,500; asking prices on dealer cars run $26,000-$42,000. This car's 64k miles and rare-ish colour combination sit in the upper half of that band, but a disclosed 2011 airbag-deployment accident, an undocumented cooling/AOS history and no borescope are exactly the things that should be priced as a discount, not paid for. It sold for $28,000 here in October 2022 and has gained 1,000 miles and a misfire repair since. Anything in the upper 20s is paying a scope-verified price for an unscoped car.

mission_fit.rationale: As a future keeper the shape is right: a numbers-matching-spec manual 987.1 Cayman S in a desirable colour with a clean over-rev report is a car to own for a decade. But the profile is explicit that a 3.4 S is bought ONLY with unusually strong engine due diligence, and the single mandatory item is absent. It is also the wrong instrument for the immediate problem — it does not relieve the 335i situation cheaply, and a high-20s purchase plus a Porsche-specialist maintenance budget conflicts with the cash-preservation posture implied by accelerated_bridge mode. This is attractive only as a keeper, and only if the scope comes back clean.

logistics.rationale: Modesto is roughly a two-and-a-half-hour drive from Carmel — a same-day round trip with no flight or transport needed. It is a California car with a fresh passed emissions test and all OBD monitors ready, so registration is trivial. The dealer answered questions within hours, ran the DME report on request, posted extra receipts, and explicitly offered local viewing and additional photos or video; the car is stored indoors on a tender. The only constraint is the calendar: an independent Porsche-specialist borescope has to be booked and completed before 10:56am Pacific on September 17, and the dealer has not yet agreed to release the car for an outside PPI.

emotional_spec_fit.rationale: Lapis Blue Metallic over Stone Gray with the Preferred Package Plus, bi-xenons, heated seats and the deployable spoiler is a genuinely handsome, well-optioned 987.1 — and the photos back it up, with red calipers behind clean silver 18s and an unfussy stock stance. A six-speed manual mid-engined Porsche coupe is squarely in the enthusiast brief and far more special than the MINI/GTI bridge candidates. Only the documented accident history, however minor and however honestly disclosed, keeps this from a 10 for a car intended to be kept.

what_would_change_verdict: An independent Porsche-specialist borescope with retained photos showing clean cylinder walls in 4-6 (and 1-3) would satisfy the hard gate and move this from unbuyable to a serious keeper candidate.
Production of the pre-2024 records showing water pump, AOS and coolant pipe work, plus a post-repair confirmation that the May 2026 misfire is gone, would materially lift documentation and condition.
A hammer in the low-to-mid 20s rather than the high 20s, reflecting the disclosed airbag-deployment accident and the unscoped engine, would make the risk-adjusted price defensible.
Scope photos showing scoring in any cylinder, or the dealer declining an outside PPI before the close, would end this immediately.
Evidence that the misfire recurs, or live-data showing per-cylinder misfire counts climbing, would end this immediately.
evidence.mission_note: As a future keeper this is the right car in the wrong evidentiary state: a manual 987.1 Cayman S in Lapis Blue with a clean over-rev report is exactly what the keeper brief describes, but the profile is unambiguous that no borescope means no Cayman S, and nobody — original owner included — has ever looked. It also does nothing for the accelerated_bridge problem and, at a likely high-20s hammer plus Porsche-specialist upkeep, works against the cash-preservation posture the 335i replacement calls for.
evidence.rationale: Hard gate unmet: there is no borescope on this 3.4 M97, and the original owner states in the comments that he never had one done, resting instead on no smoke and no oil consumption — precisely the symptom-based reassurance that counts as zero evidence here. Everything else about the car is better than average. The VIN-matched Autel DME scan is a genuinely good result (Ranges 4-6 all zero, one Range-3 stamp roughly 877 operating hours ago out of 1,827 total), the seller volunteered the 2011 accident that Carfax does not show and published the repair order, and three independent-shop invoices corroborate the odometer chain from 63,018 to 63,630. But those same invoices show what is absent: no water pump, no AOS, no coolant pipes, no clutch, nothing before 2024 despite the claim of records from new. They also show a cylinder 1 and 3 misfire diagnosed on 09 May 2026, four months before the auction, fixed with a camshaft solenoid, sensor, six coils and plugs, with no document proving it stayed fixed — and that sits uncomfortably beside a seller who writes that no work was needed. The dealer's own checklist contradicts the February invoice on both brake pads (7/6mm versus 4mm to sensor) and tires after some 400 miles, which weakens the one inspection on offer. Comps put good 987.1 S manuals between $23,250 and $29,500, so the current $5,105 is an opening bid and nothing more. Logistics are excellent — Modesto is a short drive, the smog is fresh, the seller is responsive — which is exactly why the borescope should be booked rather than the risk accepted.
